# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1143 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/emergent-biological-capabilities-in
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Adi Mashiach
- arXiv: 2611.14504
- Plain-English subtitle: AI model learns to predict how drugs bind to proteins without being taught
- Summary: Researchers trained a massive AI model called Bonbon on 3.2 trillion molecular sequences and found it spontaneously developed three new abilities it was never explicitly trained for: predicting how drugs work, pinpointing where they bind on proteins, and determining the type of chemical bonds involved. When tested in the lab on nine diseases, the model identified entirely new drug candidates that actually worked, including compounds that inhibited proteins researchers hadn't specifically trained it on.
- Why it matters: Drug discovery today is slow and expensive—identifying promising candidates can take years. Bonbon ran at five thousand times faster than current best methods while discovering genuinely novel compounds in real wet-lab experiments. If the 61.5% hit rate holds across more targets, this could dramatically accelerate the identification of new treatments for diseases where current options are limited or failing.

### DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/deepfinance-can-ai-diligence
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Drew Hahn, Tyler Shibata, Jackson Grove et al.
- arXiv: 2611.10926
- Plain-English subtitle: Can AI handle the judgment calls that make or break hundred-million-dollar deals?
- Summary: Researchers created a realistic test of whether AI can do the complex thinking required in private equity and investment banking deals worth over $100 million. The best AI model passed only 57.6% of the criteria, and it frequently made the right calculations from the wrong data or found important information without acting on it—suggesting that AI still struggles with the judgment calls that matter most in high-stakes finance.
- Why it matters: Banks and investment firms are already using AI to speed up due diligence on major deals, but this research shows these systems can confidently produce wrong answers by pulling from bad sources or ignoring critical evidence. Until AI closes this gap, dealmakers need to treat AI outputs as a starting point requiring human oversight, not as a shortcut to faster decision-making on deals where errors can cost millions.

### One Curve, Different Weights: AUC, the Brier Score, Decision-Weighted AUC, and the Policy Youden Index
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/one-curve-different-weights
- Category: Statistics
- Authors: Yegor Baranovski
- arXiv: 2611.14465
- Plain-English subtitle: Why different ways of measuring model performance rank them differently
- Summary: Two standard measures for evaluating risk prediction models—AUC and the Brier score—often disagree about which model performs better. Researchers discovered that both metrics, along with a new weighted variant, are actually different ways of averaging the same underlying curve, but they put emphasis on different parts of it depending on what matters to the person using the model.
- Why it matters: When hospitals, lenders, or other organizations choose prediction models to guide high-stakes decisions, they need metrics that reflect what actually matters to them—not generic measures that treat all situations equally. This work shows that existing metrics can hide these differences in priorities, potentially leading organizations to pick models that optimize for the wrong things. The new weighted metric lets decision-makers explicitly state what they care about and choose models accordingly.

### Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/pyrite-building-and-benchmarking
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Megha Srivastava, Michael H. Lim, Allison M. Keys et al.
- arXiv: 2611.14511
- Plain-English subtitle: Training AI to pick the right molecular shapes for drug design
- Summary: Predicting which way a drug molecule will bind to its target protein is surprisingly hard—even expert chemists with visualization tools perform barely better than guessing. Researchers created Pyrite, a benchmark of 1,500 test cases, and built two AI agents that solve this problem by reasoning about molecular geometry and learning which chemical features matter most, achieving up to 74% accuracy and outperforming human experts.
- Why it matters: Drug discovery currently wastes time and money evaluating binding poses that won't work. An AI system that reliably ranks these candidates could accelerate early-stage drug screening and reduce failed experiments, potentially shortening the timeline from molecular design to testable compounds.

### The Dose Makes the Poison: Exposure-Aware Evaluation of Generative Drug Design
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/the-dose-makes-the
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Maria Franz, N. Benjamin Erichson
- arXiv: 2611.13398
- Plain-English subtitle: Why promising drug candidates fail when you ignore how much patients must take
- Summary: Computational models that design new drug molecules often overlook a critical real-world factor: the dose patients would actually need to take. Researchers re-evaluated 60 drug candidates using realistic pharmacokinetic simulations and found that 7 couldn't deliver enough drug to the target, while 28% posed safety risks at their required dose. Most strikingly, 85% of the candidates deemed viable turned out to be worse than molecules the initial screening had dismissed.
- Why it matters: Drug companies rely on AI to narrow down millions of generated molecules into a manageable list for expensive lab testing. If the screening process ignores dose and exposure, researchers waste time and money pursuing dead ends—or worse, advance candidates that would require impractical pill sizes or dangerous safety margins. Incorporating dose-aware evaluation could redirect resources toward molecules that actually work in living bodies, not just on paper.

### Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/prediction-inference-for-hybrid
- Category: Economics
- Authors: Kyle Parrella, Kejin Wu
- arXiv: 2611.13212
- Plain-English subtitle: Measuring uncertainty in stock volatility predictions, not just point forecasts
- Summary: Researchers upgraded hybrid machine-learning models for predicting stock market volatility by adding a measure of uncertainty around each forecast—something prior work had ignored. The new approach combines ARMA statistical modeling with LSTM neural networks and uses bootstrap resampling to build prediction intervals that capture fat tails in financial data. Testing on U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025 shows the method produces intervals closer to their intended coverage levels than competing approaches.
- Why it matters: Traders and risk managers rely on volatility forecasts to price options, set position limits, and hedge portfolios. A point estimate without a confidence band is incomplete—you need to know how wrong you might be. This work delivers prediction intervals with reliable coverage, so investors can size positions appropriately rather than making decisions based on false precision.

### Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/contrastive-discovery-open-ended
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Ziang Liu, James J. Kim, Yijia Dai et al.
- arXiv: 2611.14514
- Plain-English subtitle: How AI scientists can find the right answer, not just rule one out
- Summary: When AI systems test scientific ideas, they typically check whether a hypothesis is true or false—but rejection only rules out one option, leaving many alternatives possible. Researchers show that testing against multiple competing explanations instead resolves 73% of rejected hypotheses to a specific alternative, and guides AI to answer 67% more scientific questions with the same experimental budget.
- Why it matters: As AI takes on more autonomous scientific work, moving from yes-or-no testing to hypothesis comparison could dramatically accelerate discovery by eliminating wasted experiments on dead ends. In validation tests with human experts, this approach achieved 78–82% agreement, suggesting AI systems using this method could propose ideas that real scientists would independently verify as correct.

### Cotangent-lift inference of stochastic microbial dynamics
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/cotangent-lift-inference-of
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: José A. Capitán, Alberto Megías, Cristina Sardón
- arXiv: 2611.14423
- Plain-English subtitle: Untangling real bacterial growth from measurement errors in gut samples
- Summary: When scientists measure bacteria in the gut over time, they face a puzzle: the noise from their measuring tools gets tangled with the actual bacterial dynamics. This paper shows how to separate the two by treating the true bacterial counts as hidden and using advanced statistical techniques, recovering growth rates and interaction strengths that simpler methods miss—though real microbiome data remains noisy enough that even this approach attributes most of a dominant bacterium's changes to measurement error rather than true biology.
- Why it matters: Microbiome studies rely on time-series measurements to understand how bacterial communities actually behave and interact. Current methods used in the field can't distinguish measurement noise from real biological change, leading to wrong conclusions about which bacteria are responding to treatment or changing naturally. This work provides a practical way to do that separation, potentially improving how researchers interpret whether an observed shift in a patient's microbiome is genuine or just noise in the data.

### Structure of correlations for the single-j model using quantum information theory
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/structure-of-correlations-for
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Javier Faba, Vicente Martín, Luis Robledo
- arXiv: 2611.14460
- Plain-English subtitle: How broken symmetries hide and rearrange correlations in quantum systems
- Summary: When quantum systems break symmetry to reach their lowest energy state, physicists thought this was how they maximize correlations while staying mathematically simple. By studying a realistic nuclear model, researchers found that different types of broken symmetry actually affect correlations in contradictory ways, and that restoring symmetry moves correlations between simple pairs to much more complex patterns.
- Why it matters: Understanding how correlations hide in quantum systems is essential for accurately predicting nuclear behavior and designing quantum technologies. Current approximations in nuclear physics rely on symmetry breaking to simplify calculations, but if this mechanism doesn't reliably capture correlations as expected, physicists may need to rethink which approximations are trustworthy for real predictions.

### Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/causal-concept-explanations-for
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Josh Rountree, Pulkit Verma, Oswin So et al.
- arXiv: 2611.14407
- Plain-English subtitle: Making AI explanations actually prove why decisions happen
- Summary: Most AI explanations only show what matters, not whether they truly caused a decision. Researchers built CCW-Net, a new method that forces neural networks to learn concept-based explanations that are provably necessary and sufficient for their outputs—meaning a concept only gets credit for influencing a result if removing it actually changes that result. The method measures exactly how much each concept causally contributes to each decision, eliminating explanations that look right but mislead.
- Why it matters: When autonomous systems make critical decisions—like controlling aircraft or self-driving cars—we need to trust that their explanations reflect real causal chains, not coincidences. A model might output "plane safe to fly" while a dashboard shows "fuel level normal," but if that fuel reading doesn't actually drive the decision, the explanation creates dangerous false confidence. CCW-Net fills this gap by certifying that explanations are genuinely causal, making it possible for regulators and operators to confidently evaluate whether a system is truly reasoning safely or just appearing to.
